authors: Caves EM, Brandley NC, Johnsen S
title: Visual Acuity and the Evolution of Signals (Supplemental Information: Tables S1 to S3)
why: Tables S1 to S3 hold acuity with eye size across species (S1), for 93 birds (S2) and for insects (S3), with sources; the fetch tool was refused by ScienceDirect, so only the values in the main text are logged, and every view's sharpness would gain a species-level value.

title: Supplementary Material for: Visual Acuity in Mammals: Effects of Eye Size and Ecology
journal: Figshare (supplement to Brain, Behavior and Evolution 83: 43-53)
why: Behavioural and anatomical acuity of 91 mammals with eye length and activity pattern; open under CC BY but the file sits behind a short-lived signed link the fetch tool cannot follow; would set sharpness for cat, dog, deer, rabbit, squirrel, mammal, primate and bat views.

authors: Inger R, Bennie J, Davies TW, Gaston KJ
title: Potential biological and ecological effects of flickering artificial light (Table 3 and Table S1)
why: Flicker fusion of 81 species with light levels; Table 3 is an image and the Table S1 spreadsheet was refused (HTTP 429), so most values build 22 cites from it could not be re-read; would fix every view's pace and its light dependence.

title: Seeing better at night: life style, eye design and the optimum strategy of spatial and temporal summation
why: Gives the optimal spatial and temporal pooling for each light level from eye parameters, which is the model the dim-light simulation of section 1.7 needs for every nocturnal view.

title: Fast and slow photoreceptors — a comparative study of the functional diversity of coding and conductances in the Diptera
why: Photoreceptor speed (corner frequencies, integration times) across flies, which would set the time constant of the insect views' temporal filter from measurements.

title: Mammalian retinal specializations for high acuity vision evolve in response to both foraging strategies and morphological constraints (Supplementary Table S1)
why: The article is open; its Supplementary Table S1 classifies retinal specializations (area centralis, horizontal streak, vertical streak, fovea) in 82 mammals, which would give each mammal view its resolution map.

authors: Caves EM, Sutton T, Johnsen S
title: Visual acuity in ray-finned fishes correlates with eye size and habitat
why: A compilation of fish acuity with eye size; open (CC BY-NC-ND) but the journal and the Duke repository both answered with bot checks; would set the fish view's sharpness by family and give a size rule for unmeasured species.

title: Evolution of vertebrate visual pigments
why: A compilation of vertebrate cone and rod pigments; would give reptiles, crocodilians, amphibians and fish their receptor peaks, which none of the compilations read here covers.

title: Visual fields and their functions in birds
why: Bird visual fields and binocular overlap by group; would replace the guessed field of view in the bird, wader and hawk views.

title: Apposition compound eyes (chapter 7 of Animal Eyes, 2nd edition)
why: Only chapters 1 to 3 (to p. 65) of the Drive copy came through; chapter 7 covers sampling, acute zones and resolution of compound eyes, the basis of the insect lattice in section 1.8.

title: Movements of the eyes (chapter 9 of Animal Eyes, 2nd edition)
why: Saccades, scanning and head movements across animals, which the engine's gaze controller needs; did not come through the Drive copy.

title: Superposition eyes (chapter 8 of Animal Eyes, 2nd edition)
why: Optics and sensitivity of superposition eyes (moths, beetles, crustaceans), needed for the dim-light model of nocturnal insects and crustaceans; did not come through the Drive copy.

title: Receptor noise as a determinant of colour thresholds
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
why: The original receptor-noise model with its noise values for bees, birds and people; the formula is confirmed through Clark and colleagues 2017, but the noise values the colour scaling of section 1.2 would use are not; PubMed Central answered with a robot check.

authors: Potier S, Lieuvin M, Pfaff M, Kelber A
title: How fast can raptors see?
why: The primary source for the hawk view's flicker values, which build 22 cites through a university press release; the journal answered with a bot check.

title: Scaling of visual acuity with body size in mammals and birds
why: A scaling rule from eye or body size to acuity, which would let the app infer sharpness for unmeasured mammals and birds.

authors: Carleton KL, Escobar-Camacho D, Stieb SM, Cortesi F, Marshall NJ
title: Seeing the rainbow: mechanisms underlying spectral sensitivity in teleost fishes
why: A review of fish cone peaks and filters; would set the fish view's colour matrix by habitat.

title: Temporal acuity of honeybee vision: behavioural studies using flickering stimuli
why: The primary source of the honeybee's 200 Hz in bright light, which build 22's bee row quotes through Inger and colleagues.

title: The flicker fusion frequencies of six laboratory insects, and the response of the compound eye to mains fluorescent ‘ripple’
why: Insect flicker fusion with light levels (the tsetse fly's 286 Hz at 300 lux among them), for the insect view's pace.

authors: Govardovskii VI, Fyhrquist N, Reuter T, Kuzmin DG, Donner K
title: In search of the visual pigment template
why: The template used in sections 1.2 and 2, here taken from pavo's implementation; reading the paper would confirm the constants.

title: Modelling oil droplet absorption spectra and spectral sensitivities of bird cone photoreceptors
why: The oil droplet model pavo uses, needed to build bird receptor curves from a sheet's λmax values.

authors: Stevens M, Párraga CA, Cuthill IC, Partridge JC, Troscianko TS
title: Using digital photography to study animal coloration
journal: Biological Journal of the Linnean Society
why: The original tests of mapping camera RGB to bird and human cone catches, background to section 2.

authors: Stürzl W, Boeddeker N, Dittmar L, Egelhaaf M
title: Mimicking honeybee eyes with a 280° field of view catadioptric imaging system
why: A camera built to sample like a bee's eyes; its sampling scheme could guide the bee view's field and resolution map.

title: Polarization distance: a framework for modelling object detection by polarization vision systems
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
why: How to turn polarization measurements into a contrast an animal would detect; background for any polarization effect.

authors: Kelber A, Vorobyev M, Osorio D
title: Animal colour vision — behavioural tests and physiological concepts
journal: Biological reviews of the Cambridge Philosophical Society
why: Which animals have behavioural evidence of colour vision and of what dimensionality, background for the colour rows; listed as open on figshare but not reached.
